blocks.text: The electronics sit in a black steel box on the robot: the XMachines **XT_PS V1.0** control board carrying an **STM32 Nucleo-32**, a perfboard with optocouplers and resistors, an 8-channel logic-level shifter, and the cable conduits to the drives, the battery and the sprayer. The boards are glued and wired in place, so this chapter shows them as 3-D renders built in MATLAB from the photos (`docs/report/build/figtools/real_electronics_3d.m`). Part packages have their standard sizes; positions, silkscreen labels and colours follow the photos, and part functions are inferred from the silkscreen and the wiring.

blocks.text: The XT_PS board takes the 48 V battery voltage at its `+48V_IN` connector and makes its own low voltage with an on-board buck regulator. Two CAN connectors on its left edge lead to a transceiver (U3); two optocouplers (U5, U7) isolate digital inputs. The Nucleo-32 plugs into female headers whose pin labels (A0-A7, D13, 3V3, 5V, VIN) are printed on the board ({fig:M50_xt_ps_board_3d.png}).

blocks.caption: XT_PS V1.0 control board with the STM32 Nucleo-32 (3-D render after electronics_box_xt_ps_nucleo.jpeg).

blocks.text: The firmware of the main controller is modelled in `Shaddad_MCU` as rate-monotonic tasks, as it would run on the STM32: `Task_1k` (1 ms) decodes the SBUS frames and runs the watchdog, `Task_5` (5 ms) reads the IMU and estimates tilt and yaw rate, `Task_10` (10 ms) maps the RC channels and runs the safety supervisor, the mode manager and the vehicle control, and `Task_50` (50 ms) scales the ADC inputs and runs the implement functions. Every signal between tasks passes a rate transition, as in the generated code. For the real robot the speed limits were changed to 1.4 m/s in MANUAL, 1.2 m/s in AUTO and 1.70 m/s overspeed. The mode manager in `Task_10` decides when the robot may drive ({fig:F20_mcu_modes.png}): it arms only from STANDBY with neutral sticks and all safety conditions met, and every stop needs a new arm edge.

blocks.caption: Mode manager of the firmware model (fw_mode_manager in Task_10): Phase 1 transitions.

blocks.text: The firmware model was built for an STM32H743 target. The chip of the real Nucleo-32 and of the USB-C board is not yet known (open item 5 in {sec:mb10_open}); the simulation does not depend on it, and code generation will be retargeted once the chip is confirmed.

Next to the control board sit a blue STM32 core board with a USB-C connector, BOOT0, NRST and KEY buttons and an LQFP48 microcontroller, and a red FT232RL USB-UART adapter with its 3.3 / 5 V jumper ({fig:M51_stm32_ftdi_3d.png}). The CUR header on the board below takes the current sensor.

blocks.caption: STM32 USB-C core board and FT232RL USB-UART adapter on the control board (3-D render after electronics_ftdi_stm32_board.jpeg and electronics_ftdi_closeup.jpg).

blocks.text: An ADS1115 / ADS1015 module adds four 16-bit analog inputs over I2C ({fig:M52_ads1115_3d.png}). The LM2596 buck module ({fig:M53_lm2596_3d.png}) makes a 5 V rail; its bottom side is rendered as photographed, the top side with the usual component layout of this module.

blocks.caption: ADS1115 / ADS1015 ADC module on the control board (3-D render after electronics_ads1115_adc.jpg).
LM2596 DC-DC buck module: top side with the usual layout of this module (left) and bottom side as in electronics_lm2596_buck.jpg (right).

blocks.text: The XMachines SPR V1.3 board drives the sprayer. The photo shows part of it: 1 % metal-film resistors, a 4-pin SMD package, an axial diode and two capacitors next to the board name ({fig:M54_spr_board_3d.png}).

blocks.caption: Detail of the XMachines SPR V1.3 sprayer board (3-D render after electronics_xmachines_spr_v1_3_board.jpg).
